articles.title: Ocarina of Time is even better if you use a smartphone app
articles.summary: Nintendo’s Zelda Notes app for Ocarina of Time has maps and tips that make tracking down Golden Skulltulas a whole lot easier.
articles.body: I never liked hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The game has 100 of them tucked all over Hyrule, and even over my many hours with the N64 classic growing up, I can’t remember ever actually finding all of them, or even wanting to. Jumping into the Ocarina of Time remake, I expected to ignore the Golden Skulltulas once again. But while poking around Nintendo’s Zelda Notes companion app, I discovered that its maps are a huge help to tracking down all of the elusive golden spiders — and pretty much every other collectible in the game — and now I find myself constantly opening up the app to make sure I haven’t missed a secret. Inside Zelda Notes, which is available in the free Nintendo Switch app (you don’t need a Switch Online subscription to use it), you can peruse a big map of Hyrule and tap on individual areas for a closer look. The app offers just enough direction to nudge me toward an elusive pickup; when zoomed in, the app drops icons on the map showing you the locations of different collectibles, and if you tap on an icon, the app will show a popup noting any items or special requirements you need to fulfill to be able to obtain it. There are also a bunch of filters you can apply, like swapping between the maps for child and adult Link and toggling categories of icons on and off. [Image: I have a few things left to find in the Kokiri Forest. For Skulltula hunting, the map has already saved my sanity many times. While exploring, I’ll often come across the telltale Golden Skulltula sound but have no idea how to get to the tricky spider, even with the help of additional chimes from the new Echo Gem Skulltula tracking item. But with a peek at the Zelda Notes app, I can pinpoint the exact location of where the Skulltula is supposed to be and if I need to use a certain item or change the time of day to be able to get to it. I recently delved into the Shadow Temple, for example, and I couldn’t figure out how to get up to a Skulltula that I saw while coming down an elevator. But when I checked the icon on the Zelda Notes map, it said that I needed the Scarecrow Song to create a hookshot point, which I hadn’t gotten yet. As soon as I finished the dungeon, getting the Scarecrow Song was my first priority. Zelda Notes has been useful for tracking down Pieces of Heart, too, which give Link more health once you collect enough. While running up and down Zora’s River, I kept seeing two Pieces of Heart on faraway ledges that I couldn’t figure out how to get to. (My memories of my extensive time with Ocarina of Time as a kid also failed me.) But tapping one of the icons on the Zelda Notes map revealed that I needed a Cucco to get to it — and suddenly, I understood why there was one of the chirping white birds near the entrance of the zone. Yes, it can be annoying to have to open my phone and dig through an app to track down all of the Skulltulas and other objects of curiosity scattered around Hyrule. I play video games to try and get away from my phone, not look at it more. And sure, I could just look up an online guide, but that often means wading through walkthroughs of varying quality, trusting an AI summary, or scrubbing through a YouTube video. But with Zelda Notes, I’m usually in and out relatively quickly, putting down my phone after seeing a clue or an icon that pushes me in the direction of the next golden spider. I’ve already found more than 70 Golden Skulltulas, and to my surprise, I now want to hunt for the full 100.

articles.title: Tekken Legend Katsuhiro Harada Says He Wishes 'Hardware Like the Xbox Series S Wouldn't Be Released'
articles.summary: Tekken development legend Katsuhiro Harada had some strong comments for Microsoft's lower-powered Xbox Series S console, dubbing it a "weaker child" with "awkwardly lower performance."
articles.body:
Tekken development legend Katsuhiro Harada had some strong comments for Microsoft's lower-powered Xbox Series S console, dubbing it a "weaker child" with "awkwardly lower performance."

A number of video game developers have struggled with the Xbox Series S while following Microsoft's feature parity rules across Xbox Series consoles. Baldur's Gate 3 famously came to Xbox a few months late and required the help of Microsoft's engineers to get the game's split-screen co-op working on Series S . More recently, the developer of breakout shooter Wardogs admitted that the limitations of the Xbox Series S had stopped it from adding certain things to the game .

Indeed, one of the questions facing Microsoft ever since the release of the Xbox Series S back in 2020 is whether it would be willing to allow developers and publishers to release a game on Xbox Series X only, leaving Xbox Series S behind. As it stands, Xbox mandates that video games launch on both or none at all, and that there should be main feature parity between each version.

In a roundtable discussion held at the Console Game Developers Conference in Korea, Harada slammed the Series S and attempted to encourage Cyberpunk 2077 associate game director Paweł Sasko to join in the pile-on, too.

"There's something I really want to say while I have the floor," Harada began (thanks, Inven Global ), "since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released (laughs)."

Throughout his years in charge of Tekken, Harada has become known as a colorful character happy to express his opinions freely. And, to be fair, it sounds like Harada made the comment knowing he was being rather cheeky. But the developer then continued to explain his position further — and have Sasko back him up, following reports that CD Projekt struggled with Cyberpunk 2077's Series S version.

"I want to ask director Paweł personally," Harada continued. "Honestly, weren't you upset inside because of Series S?"

"It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly," Sasko responded, appearing to tiptoe around the subject.

"You just used a very polite and elegant way to say 'Xbox Series S sucks,' right?" Harada ploughed on. "Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child."

Gosh. Tell us what you really think, Harada!

"Furthermore," he continued further, "in markets like the U.S., there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

While Harada's comments will likely not come as a shock to many developers who have been tasked with releasing games across the Xbox Series family this generation, it is rare to hear someone of Harada's prominence discussing the Series S' drawbacks out loud.

In response — and in a continued attempt to not say anything that would get him in trouble — Sasko acknowledged that such Series S drawbacks were real, but that the console also offered a lot of positives. Its more affordable price point meant that developers could get their games played by a wider audience, Sasko offered, while opimtization breakthroughs initially made for Series S had also benefited Cyberpunk 2077 across all platforms.

Acknowledging Sasko's more positive take, Harada concluded that he was now worried Microsoft would "feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

Will Xbox release a lower-powered Helix console? It's unclear. After earlier reports that suggested the new console was reportedly targeting a holiday 2027 launch , more recent estimates have pointed to a 2028 launch for the machine — at an eyewatering $1,200 - $1,800 price point . Maybe that will make Harada reconsider?

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: How Skyrim Found a Second Life As Cozy Game
articles.summary: 15 years after release, Skyrim's icy, dangerous world feels warm and cozy. But why has this dark fantasy become such a comfort play? We spoke to experts and developers to find out.
articles.body:
Every few months, some YouTube channel will upload a video essay asking why we continue to play Skyrim more than a decade after release. Virtually all of them come to the same conclusion: at this point, what keeps us coming back for more isn’t the gameplay, or the story, or the seemingly never-ending wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel , but the coziness of its setting.

At a glance, this makes perfect sense. After all, many of us no longer play Skyrim to progress the narrative or complete quests, but simply to spend time in its world. And yet, if you really think about it, it’s also kind of strange. Many cozy games are devoid of danger or pressure, and sport a warm, colorful, often cartoonish look. Skyrim, on the other hand, is dark fantasy 101, its lands frozen over and filled with scary, pointy things that can and will kill you if given the chance.

Sure, some use mods that remove enemies, shake up mechanics, and even clear up the weather, making the game look and feel more similar to cozy favorites like Animal Crossing or Stardew Valley . However, I don’t think I’m alone when I say that – to me – the base game already feels incredibly cozy as it is, dragons and all. For many years I’ve wondered why. And this month, in honor of Skyrim’s 15th anniversary, I took a stab at finding answers.

While researching, it quickly became clear that most of the common reasons for Skyrim’s coziness do not hold up to scrutiny. Yes, the game’s awe-inspiring landscapes and Jeremy Soule’s soundtrack definitely play a role, but I believe it’s only a supporting one. Otherwise, why would I feel a similar kind of coziness playing games like Bioshock or Batman: Arkham City, which look and sound completely different?

“Nostalgia,” you might say, and many do. But that doesn’t quite cut it either. While the world of Skyrim has indeed become like an old friend, and booting up the game reminds me of the carefree teenage years that coincided with my initial playthrough, the coziness I feel today is – for the most part – the same coziness I remember feeling back then.

The nostalgia factor connects to another, and in my opinion equally insufficient explanation: player competence. The more we play a game, the better we get, and the easier, less threatening, and therefore cozier said game should become. Again, not my experience. For me, playing with a heavily underleveled character, so that even the most ordinary enemy encounter becomes an existential threat, actually makes the game feel more cozy, not less. Strange right?

Not really, it turns out. While early reports on the design of cozy games connected coziness to an absence of danger, today we understand the relationship to be a bit more complicated. In an article about the rise of “dark” cozy games like Dredge and Cult of the Lamb , which play around with mechanics that scare, stress, or unsettle, Polish media scholar Agata Waszkiewicz argued that danger and coziness don’t necessarily cancel each other out. Quite the contrary, designers can in fact use one to amplify the other.

“Coziness is a tricky concept to define,” Waszkiewicz tells IGN, “so we often do it by juxtaposing it with something that clearly is not cozy. There’s a reason everyone always talks about being wrapped up in a blanket, drinking tea or hot cocoa, while it is pouring outside. That contrast between outside and inside makes coziness more pronounced and easier to grasp.”

“A cabin feels warm because of the blizzard,” agrees Rachel Kowert, a research psychologist who specializes in games and mental health. The psychology of cozy games make her think of something called Prospect-Refuge theory, which basically argues that people are evolutionarily “drawn to spaces where we can see out over the world while also being sheltered from it.”

FromSoftware games have clear equivalents of prospect-refuge points in the forms of bonfires, lamps, and sites of grace: locations that shield players from enemies, even when they’re standing right beside you, while also allowing you to level up, replenish resources, and prepare for the journey ahead. Our prehistoric ancestors would have surely been able to relate.

Skyrim may not have bonfires, but its world likewise contains plenty of places where players are in proximity to yet safe from threats. Think of when you’re passing over one of the province’s many mountaintops and see a dragon flying overhead, or a giant herding his mammoths down below. For me, these are precisely the moments when the game’s world strikes me as most peaceful, and Soule’s soundtrack most relaxing.

Mark Teare, an effects artist who has since left Bethesda and is now working on a cozy game of his own, can think of another reason for why Skyrim evokes such strong feelings of coziness in players: ants. Yes, there are ants in this game, and Teare is the one who put them there, despite Bethesda’s initial protests.

“My boss saw them and was like, ‘No one is ever going to see them. Why are we wasting time on this?’” he tells IGN. “But for me they were a big deal, precisely because they were so small. Once you notice them, the world just feels so much bigger. You wonder: how many other things am I walking by and not even seeing?”

This rationale touches on a number of things that are integral to cozy game design, including presence and connection. Cozy games often encourage players to slow down and appreciate things that in other types of games they might overlook or take for granted. Details like Teare’s insects also create a sense of intimacy. Not with other players, but with the developers: “These little details didn’t need to be there, but their presence shows players that we cared, and they feel that.”

Soule once said a very similar thing, stating in an old interview that he wanted the game’s music to be a constant companion. His goal wasn’t to feed into the game’s power fantasy, but make the player “not feel alone” and “like there’s meaning to what they’re doing.” Whether you’re an expert on Elder Scrolls lore or not, his ethereal soundtrack gives you a sense that some or other god is watching over you, and that – despite the chaos of civil war and the coming of Alduin – everything in this world is fundamentally in harmony.

Speaking to Teare, I stumbled upon my third and perhaps most compelling explanation for Skyrim ’s coziness: the fact that Bethesda didn’t intend for the game to feel cozy at all. “I was down in the trenches, so I’m not sure what the big, big plans were,” he says, “but I don’t remember any discussion or mandate or anything, and none of us were actively thinking about coziness while working.”

During our conversation, Teare brought up ASMR – a sensation closely related to coziness, and hugely influential to his ongoing projects. While there are lots of successful ASMR content creators out there, many aficionados will tell you that the most potent ASMR is created unintentionally . “When someone is trying hard, it feels manufactured,” says Teare. In his opinion, the best “ASMRtists” are “really good actors” that make what they’re doing seem natural even though it’s not.

You could make a similar argument about coziness, and I think mine is pretty solid. Research on cozy game design often mentions words like the Danish hygge and Dutch gezelligheid , both of which are frequently translated into English as coziness. As a Dutch person, I can say with authority that gezelligheid isn’t something you can just force into existence. Like at a great party where everyone gets along with everyone, true gezelligheid happens when the stars align, and everything feels alright in the world – all without you having to do anything…kind of like when you’re playing Skyrim , right?

As Waszkiewicz said, coziness is tricky to define. Not only because what constitutes as cozy differs from person to person, but also because no two games are cozy in the exact same way. I’m not trying to have the final word on this subject. My only goal was to try to articulate what makes Skyrim cozy to me, and what sets this coziness apart from other games. If you feel differently, let me know in the comments. I’d love to hear.

Tim Brinkhof is a freelance writer specializing in art and history. After studying journalism at NYU, he has gone on to write for Vox, Vulture, Slate, Polygon, GQ, Esquire and more.

articles.title: Lanterns Writer Says 'Nothing's Cancelled. Calm Down' Amid Concern for Season 2 Following Shock DC Shakeup
articles.summary: Lanterns writer addresses concern over Season 2 amid DC shakeup.
articles.body:
Is Lanterns Season 2 happening or not? It’s unclear, following the shock exit of DC Studios co-CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran. Yesterday, Variety reported that Lanterns "didn't get renewed for a second season," then updated the wording of its article to say the show "has yet to be renewed for a second season."

With Skydance and new DC boss Jeremy Latcham now in charge of all intellectual property under Warner Bros.’s banner, the future of the DCU is up in the air. Gunn’s own Man of Tomorrow and Matt Reeves’ The Batman Part II (the latter of which is not part of the DCU canon) still have theatrical release dates, but beyond that, what’s the plan? We don’t know.

Lanterns , which stars Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, was well-received, and reports indicated a team had been assembled to write and produce Season 2, should it be greenlit. Here’s what Variety had to say about Lanterns, specifically:

DC Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

“Lanterns, their first live-action TV show, had strong viewership and averaged 19 million viewers globally per episode going into the finale. Yet an insider at the company suggests the crime drama isn’t quite capturing the zeitgeist, pointing out the show has yet to be renewed for a second season.”

That doesn’t sound good for Lanterns Season 2, although we know Pierre’s John Stewart is set to star in next summer’s Man of Tomorrow. Countering the doom and gloom around Lanterns, however, is Chris Cantwell, co-creator of Halt and Catch Fire. He was drafted in to work on Lanterns Season 2 as a writer, producer, and showrunner, were it to actually happen, and he’s been vocal about the reports about the series fate on social media .

“Dear Internet,” he began. “I haven’t heard a f***ing thing. People sometimes wonder what future seasons of Halt and Catch Fire would’ve been. They would’ve arrived at social media and AI and the characters would’ve killed themselves.

That sounds definitive, but as mentioned, neither James Gunn nor Jeremy Latcham have confirmed Season 2 is actually happening. Last month, then DC Studios co-CEO Peter Safran told IGN that a decision on Lanterns Season 2 would be made by the end of 2026 .

Safran confirmed there was a writer's room hashing out ideas for the future of Lanterns , but it would all depend on whether or not they come up with a good enough story worthy of following up the first season. He noted that TV was an important part of DC's future, but that they were waiting to see if there was a story worth telling before giving the greenlight to Lanterns Season 2.

"The episodic world is always going to be a really important part of our overall slate, it's a great way to tell stories that need more real estate than a feature film can offer you, and it's a great way to introduce characters that we then bring into the feature world," said Safran. "And I think that Aaron Pierre and John Stewart are a perfect example of that. We introduced him in Lanterns, and audiences will see him next summer in Man of Tomorrow. So, it's really important to us in continuing to tell aspects of the story that we're not telling in the feature film world, so there's more to come.

"Listen, we'll see what happens with Lanterns Season 2. If, I think, the collective group of HBO and DC and Chris Mundy and the team all feel like we've got something that is a worthy successor to quite a beloved first season of television, then I wouldn't be surprised to see more."

But that was last month, and a lot has happened since then.

In the wake of the DC news, the Hollywood trades have reported that Skydance wasn't particularly impressed by the box office returns of Gunn's DCU, with even Superman apparently failing to do big enough numbers .

Predictably, fans of Zack Snyder’s DCEU have called for the Snyderverse to return , reinstating, for example, Henry Cavill as Superman and continuing where Snyder’s Justice League left off. There is no indication that Skydance will do so, but that hasn’t stopped fans comparing the box office returns of four years of the Snyderverse and four years of Gunn’s DCU.

articles.title: There Are Puzzles Well Worth Solving in the New Series The Good Daughter, Starring Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy
articles.summary: Review: Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne provide the good stuff for The Good Daughter.
articles.body:
This is a non-spoiler review for all six episodes of The Good Daughter, which premieres November 12 on Peacock.

Yes, another "Good" series has entered the chat (see also: Place, Wife, Fight, Doctor, Girls, more).

The Good Daughter, developed and written by Karin Slaughter and based on her own book, is an awesome Appalachian trauma drama. Starring Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy (The White Lotus, Drop) as estranged sisters, both lawyers, trying to get to the bottom of a high school shooting in their nasty, crooked Georgia hometown, the series is quite riveting. The main mystery, involving the aforementioned shooter, has a decent enough resolution, but it's the two sisters themselves, and a massively tragic shared event from their childhood, that infuses the show with complexity and poignancy.

The Peacock series has all the ingredients you need for a cracking small town whodunit, from a great ensemble to old family feuds to haunted secrets. It checks many boxes. And while it occasionally lapses into mystery genre cliches, it has enough unique subversive elements to keep it from getting stuck in the mud.

The two sisters, Sam and Charlie Quinn, are the heart and spine of the story, and what helps elevate it over many of its homespun crime peers. It's easy to see the trope-y architecture of one sister having abandoned the town for the big city and the other staying behind, or that the one who now resides in Manhattan is rigid and the one keeping the home fires burning is a wild child. But it's deeper than that. Byrne and Fahy are magnificent here as two women who are both, at once, right and wrong. Who are both justified and unreasonable. They deliver a palpable, gripping sibling relationship filled with recognizable pain, joy, and snark.

Byrne will be the star viewers are most familiar with here, having been in big spotlight projects ever since she broke through with American audiences on FX's Damages 20 years ago. As older sister Sam, Byrne embodies a ferocious warmth amidst a shattered body, all stemming from a nightmarish home invasion targeting her father when she was in high school. Sam is a living physical reminder of the fatal events that took her mother's life, as the show keenly dissects how people are often forced to reinvent their paths and plans and mourn their old selves. She's excellent, as usual.

Fahy is the anchor of the show, however, as The Good Daughter provides a wonderful opportunity to catch her in an incredible showcase performance. There's a chance you've seen her in past projects, but it wasn't until her Emmy nomination for The White Lotus that her profile truly lifted. And Blumhouse's ridiculous (but very fun) Drop from 2025 was also a great display of her talent. As younger sis Charlie, Fahy exhibits a vulnerable stubbornness, having grown up in the wake of a tragedy afraid to let those around her know just how much it damaged and affected her for fear of taking up space in front of those who suffered more. Charlie stayed behind, in fictional Pikeville, GA, despite Sam's attempts to wrestle her free, following in her father's footsteps as a local defense attorney-slash-pariah. She's the catalyst for the story, and also, in a way, its endgame.

The Quinn family exists in the crosshairs of their witch hunt-y neighbors, often maligned for father Rusty's legal defense of those guilty of heinous crimes. Brendan Gleeson's Rusty is a gem of an erudite, boozy blowhard. Easy to love, hard to live with, he's sly, steadfast, and plays the role of the fool as tactic. He rushes to the aid of teen Kelly (Shayna Benardo) after she's arrested for gunning down her principal and a classmate not because he thinks she's innocent, but because he knows the particulars of Pikeville and how ghoulish and corrupt the local mechanisms are.

Sisters Charlie and Sam entertain Rusty's latest bootless errand, and this is how our major players all converge. Still, though, it's past revelations that allow The Good Daughter to thrive. The Quinns' reunion comes with therapy, clarity, and the ghosts of that fateful afternoon, decades earlier, when everyone's life shattered. This offers up the true stratigraphy of The Good Daughter.

The surrounding ensemble is also worthy of praise, from Harper Steele's trusty, sassy office manager to Michael Dorman's reliable, loving ex-hubbie to Jake McDorman's hunky local color. They, along with the rest, are always two steps to the side of being standard mystery players, constantly offering up more than expected. If you pay attention to casting, and know your character actors, then you might be able to predict the outcome of the case, but still, that being said, there are many more reveals, especially pertaining to the the Sisters Quinn, that will outshine that.

articles.title: Blizzard Changes World of Warcraft Forever Gold Rewards For High Level Quests, and Players are Celebrating
articles.summary: For the longest time in World of Warcraft, when you finished a quest at max level, the experience you would earn would get converted to gold. But in WoW Forever, Blizzard killed off that conversion, and has now added a fix.
articles.body:
For the longest time in World of Warcraft, when you finished a quest at max level, the experience you would earn would get converted to gold. But in WoW Forever, Blizzard killed off that conversion, and has now added a fix.

The experience-to-gold conversion for quests completed at high level has been a part of WoW for nearly 20 years, to the point where a lot of players rely on it to build up some cash when they hit max level, especially in the Classic versions of the game. But, when WoW Forever launched last week, that conversion was missing, and now that players are starting to hit level 60, they're starting to feel that loss of gold.

Thankfully, Blizzard community manager Kaivax has posted on the WoW forum to say a hotfix will go live "in the next 24 hours or so" to help high level players earn a little bit of gold. Rather than converting experience to gold, Blizzard will buff the gold rewarded for high level quests, regardless of what level you are.

According to Kaivax: "we’re preparing a hotfix that will add additional gold rewards to most quests with a quest level of level 48 or higher, including adding gold to quests above level 48 that never previously rewarded gold at all. The idea here is that you should feel good about doing quests at the appropriate level to progress your character, and you should feel adequately rewarded with gold for doing so."

But why change that experience-gold conversion in the first place? Well, according to Kaivax, that conversion "created an incentive for players to hold a full quest log worth of completed quests to hand in after hitting level 60 for maximum gold returns. Under those conditions, the optimal way for players to level to 60 was to simply grind creatures for XP and not hand in quests at all, which is not a design we want to retain in WoW: Forever."

Kaivax's post was in a thread where players were complaining about not being able to earn gold from quests. The original post was from Faze, who said four days ago that "the change to not give additional gold in exchange for EXP at 60 needs to be reverted. Quests are basically useless at 60 if they don’t have a reward. This was one of the easy ways to make gold to afford spells and mounts. This is a horrible design and change. It feels good to complete quests and now this just feels BAD at 60. Change this back ASAP."

Before Kaivax posted, nearly 100 replies deep, there were a ton of players who were essentially saying that they'd stop playing the game over this. Player Glôwstick said: "this is a deal breaker for me, wont be playing any more until this is reverted," while Rackjaw commented: "WoW Forever devs seem to be obsessed with 'fixing' things that aren’t broken."

However, players seem to have changed their tune immediately after Kaivax's response. Danni said: "Nice change. Quests giving consistent gold whether you do them at 59 or 60 makes sense, and doesn’t punish people for handing them in 'too soon.'"

There are some players that are skeptical about the change. For instance, Jalesanda posted: "I will withhold putting the pitch forks away for now until we see how much gold this is, and how it compares. But it’s put down, for now."

This change really does highlight the philosophy that the WoW Forever team is taking with the new game mode, though. While there are players who probably want a 1:1 copy of Classic, Forever will make changes as long as they stay within the 'spirit' of the game. That's why, for instance, the devs held the line on group tagging , but had no problem adding some quests like the beloved 'Kyle's Gone Missing' or changing how dungeon experience is earned.

And as more players start to reach max level , the initial design of WoW Forever is going to be pushed to its limits, and we'll just have to see the extent of changes that Blizzard is going to be willing to make. Right now, WoW Forever is kind of like a blank canvass, and while I've been given some hints of where the game might go in the future, I can't wait to see the unique path Forever takes. And this experience to gold conversion change is really just the first of many changes I'm sure we're going to see.

articles.title: Bethesda Sets Expectations as Fans Hope for The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel News Today
articles.summary: Bethesda has issued an official response to fans expecting a major announcement for The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel at some point today.
articles.body:
Bethesda has issued an official response to fans expecting a major announcement for The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel at some point today.

In a post from the company's official account on reddit , Bethesda said it had seen the growing speculation among its fans that today, November 11, would bring more details on Sentinel, hot on the heels of the game's subtitle and logo reveal just last week .

Alas, today will not be when we find out more about the game, Bethesda has now said — pouring cold water on hopes that we would see more of the Hammerfell-set role-player anytime soon.

Despite being announced eight years ago, Sentinel is reportedly still two years away from launch — at least . We don't even know which platforms it will launch on (could it be an Xbox Helix launch title?) or whether it will be an Xbox console exclusive . Of course, that hasn't stopped Bethesda already beginning to sell Sentinel merch .

"Hey everyone, wanted to pop in to say that we aren't going to have any big announcements tomorrow," Bethesda wrote overnight (tomorrow meaning today, November 11). "We're excited you're excited but we will not be sharing anything new on Sentinel for some time."

Response to that statement is unsurprisingly a little mixed, with some fans commenting that they appreciate the clarity from Bethesda, while others joking that it will be another eight years before we see anything more of the game.

Of course, November 11 is an important date in the minds of The Elder Scrolls fans. It is the original release date for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, all the way back in 2011 (memorably, on 11/11/11). 15 years on, you can see why some had hoped Bethesda might have more to say today — but alas that is not set to be the case.

For those wanting to read more Sentinel today, however, IGN has you covered. We've got a deep dive on what Sentinel actually means based on The Elder Scrolls lore , and why Sentinel's in-universe quote teaser is sparking particular timeline speculation . We also have a roundup of former Bethesda design director Bruce Nesmith's wishes for Sentinel , whenever the long-awaited game does finally arrive.

articles.title: The DC Art of Riccardo Federici Highlights the Talented Painter
articles.summary: The mega-talented painter Riccardo Federici renders the DC Universe like no one else, and his career is now the subject of a new art book from Clover Press.
articles.body:
Clover Press is continuing its The DC Art of... series, this time with a book focused on artist and painter extraordinaire Riccardo Federici. Federici has built a strong reputation on books like The Last God and Aquaman, as well as numerous DC Comics covers. All of that work will be on full display in this latest DC Art of volume.

With the Kickstarter campaign for The DC Art of Riccardo Federici live now, IGN can exclusively reveal the Batman-themed art plates that are featured as optional extras in the campaign. Check them out in the slideshow gallery below:

The DC Art of Riccardo Federici Preview Gallery

The DC Art of Riccardo Federici is a 9" x 12" hardcover book that clocks in at over 200 pages. The book features both finished artwork as well as sketches and behind-the-scenes process material. The Kickstarter campaign includes numerous optional bonuses, including the aforementioned art plates as well as exclusive covers and collectibles.

"I've always had the need to create through drawing, painting, and sculpture, and like all self-taught artists, curiosity and experimentation have allowed me to approach a world that offers so many creative opportunities: the world of comics,” said Federici in a statement. “How you represent scenes, composition, anatomy, perspective, light and color, character acting, concept design, set design, etc. are all topics found within a single comic book interior page or cover. For me, comics are not just narration through sequential images: they are the result of reasoning explained in concrete and complex images that are the artistic expression of each author."

”I remember when Riccardo’s work first hit all of our desks at DC on Dark Nights. Incredible work, and there was much discussion as to what he’d follow it up with,” said Clover Press Publisher Hank Kanalz. “What really stood out was the work he did with Phillip Kennedy Johnson on The Last God. He really built a new world from scratch and showed what he was really capable of doing.”

Clover Press' previous DC art books include The DC Art of Jorge Jimenez , The DC Art of Michael Turner , and The DC Art of Bruno Redondo .

articles.title: 12 Days of Snoopy Exclusive Clip: Inside the Peanuts Holiday Special
articles.summary: Watch an exclusive clip from 12 Days of Snoopy on Apple TV. The creators explain the new Peanuts holiday special and Snoopy’s spot on the naughty list.
articles.body:
Charlie Brown, Snoopy, and the rest of the Peanuts have been a mainstay of Christmas going back decades. And now, more than 60 years after the debut of the A Charlie Brown Christmas, the gang is back for a new round of holiday mischief. Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy, a half-hour Peanuts holiday special, hits Apple TV on November 13 and IGN has a brand-new exclusive preview of the animated show.

As you can see in the player above, 12 Days of Snoopy focuses on the loveable beagle ending up on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, Snoopy “sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.”

The special is executive produced by Mark Evestaff and directed by Rob Boutilier, who also developed The Snoopy Show for Apple TV along with other entries in the Peanuts universe like Snoopy in Space. I spoke with Evestaff and Boutilier ahead of 12 Days of Snoopy’s release about creating a “companion piece” to the beloved holiday classic.

How Everyone’s Favorite Beagle Ended Up on Santa’s Naughty List

IGN: In the exclusive scene we’re debuting, Snoopy finds out that he's going to be on Santa's naughty list. Why did you guys decide to go in that direction?

Mark Evestaff (Executive producer): It was just sort of looking back into Snoopy's character and his mischievous nature. Sometimes he's a little self-centered, but he's also kind and caring and a good friend. And so we want to explore those emotions and basically see how the neighborhood would rally around Snoopy knowing that he would mess up when he's trying to do good. But that effort and that commitment is a bit of the takeaway from this show, getting a little help from your friends and then just trying to do the right thing.

IGN: Is it fun to get to explore Snoopy's mischievous side?

Rob Boutilier (Director): Yes, always. It's fun in the scripts, it's fun in the writer's room, but it really comes alive when we get the storyboards because that's when the artists can really go to town on it. I mean, Peanuts, I kind of always look at the classic specials. They have a fairly simple story, a simple idea to them, but it's the emotions of the characters that make it more complicated. So that idea of the naughty list and Snoopy trying to do good, we kind of knew visually there's a lot of territory we could cover there for funny and for emotional bits.

The Biggest Challenge of Following the OG Charlie Brown Christmas

IGN: It's inevitable that people are going to reflect back in one way or another on the original 1965 special. Is there anything that's particularly challenging about creating a Peanuts Christmas special when the original is so beloved?

Boutilier: When we started on Peanuts, I kind of took the viewpoint that everything we ever did is always going to be compared back to Charlie Brown Christmas, Charlie Brown’s All Stars, Great Pumpkin, the Thanksgiving special, all those big ones, because it's so generational. So the challenge is, “How do you bring a new viewer into Peanuts and also satisfy everyone else?” You can't think about it too much because it'll just overwhelm you.

So the best we can do is just make sure that we're being true to [Peanuts creator Charles] Schulz. We're being true to the characters so that 12 Days of Snoopy can sit as a companion piece to A Charlie Brown Christmas. And if you watch them both back to back, hopefully you're not going to see a lot of difference in how characters are reacting to things.

Why 2026 Is the Right Time to Combine Peanuts and Christmas Once Again

IGN: Why did you guys decide that now is the time for another Peanuts Christmas special? It’s been 60 years since the original and nearly 30 years since the last holiday special.

Evestaff: We did explore a couple of Christmas episodes in [The Snoopy Show] and honestly, we had a lot of fun just because it's so synonymous, Peanuts and Christmas. The idea was rumbling about in the writer's room that we knew had legs. And then when [Peanuts content partner] WildBrain and Apple TV approached us, they were like, "Do you have any ideas?" and we jumped at the opportunity. We knew this was sacred ground, but we also knew that with the resources we had, we could do something special.

The important thing is we didn't want to tread on anything that had been done. This really was from Snoopy's lens, from Snoopy's point of view, as a companion piece to the original.

What 12 Days of Snoopy Owes to the Original

IGN: Was there any particular scene or moment in that original Charlie Brown Christmas that you guys took direct inspiration from?

Evestaff : There are certainly inspirational moments because it's such a classic. There's certain things that just don't get done today from a voiceover point of view. When Sally talks, you could tell they would splice together [cuts] and it was just adorable and charming and they don't do that [anymore]. And so part of casting younger kids was an homage to that idea of having younger kids in these roles that are not trained actors, that are genuine and authentic kids in that performance.

IGN: How did you update the animation style while still remaining true to the original?

Boutilier: I would love it if we could make it look even more passive, but I just don't think people would [accept it]. It'd be nice to put cell shadows on stuff every so often as a joke, but it just wouldn't fly in terms of standards for what we watch. But when we developed The Snoopy Show, part of it was to not only honor Schulz's work, but to also honor [A Charlie Brown Christmas director Bill] Melendez's work because we wanted to make sure that there was a comfortability of it where people would watch it and go, "Okay, this is the Peanuts I remember. They haven't wrecked it." So we kind of approached it that way, even with storyboards like, “Okay, how would they have done this in the '60s?”

Sometimes we follow it, sometimes we'd break new ground, but it was always thinking like, “Okay, it's got to be the way it was before, before we can gently push it forward.”

Why the Peanuts Holiday Specials Are Still Popular

IGN: Is there any one thing that you can point to as to why these Peanuts Christmas stories still endure?

Evestaff: There is that universal appeal to these characters that we see ourselves in one of these kids or in Snoopy. It goes back to Charles Schulz and the design of these characters and how, over the years, he was able to battle test them through his strips and evolve them. They're so whittled down and so pure of design. [There’s] just something that's universal when you see it.

Boutilier: I think there's an emotional attachment that comes with the Peanuts and it extends beyond the strip. So even if it's as simple as someone cutting out a strip and putting it on the fridge, they're putting it on the fridge for a reason. And same goes for the specials. Charlie Brown Christmas is a tradition. Every year people are wondering, “Where is it? Where can I watch it for free?” Hopefully something like 12 Days of Snoopy can be annual viewing for younger generations..

articles.title: Netflix's The Body Is a Satirical Sermon on Catholic School Full of Partying, Sex (and Sexual Repression), and Religious Mania
articles.summary: The Body, titled “Slutty God,” opens with a Bible verse about, well, the body. Series creator Quinn Shephard picks apart that verse, disseminating a sermon that reflects on pleasure, purity, sacrifice, and how one part affects the whole. Outside of the divinity school existentialism, though, The Body is first and foremost a wild and funny drama/satire about a Catholic school dance team whose bad decisions at a Halloween party hazing ritual leads to mass hysteria.
articles.body:
The Body is streaming on Netflix now. This is a non-spoiler review of the full first season.

The first episode of The Body, titled “Slutty God,” opens with a Bible verse: “Now you are Christ’s body and every one of you is a part of it.” After watching all eight episodes of the new Netflix Catholic high school drama/satire/fever dream, it’s clear that series creator Quinn Shephard did the the extra reading on that passage from First Corinthians 12: “And God has placed in the church first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and of different kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?”

The Body dabbles in all of the above, literally and metaphorically. Going too deep on it will quickly get into spoiler territory, but The Body mounts a sermon — in the fallout of a high school dance team’s hazing ritual gone wrong — about, well, the body. Is it for pleasure, for purity, for sacrifice? Is it a vessel? What happens when it, both as an individual, or as a parochial community, becomes ill or becomes susceptible to magical thinking? How does one affect the whole?

But let me pull back on the divinity school existentialism here, because while The Body wrestles with all of those things, it is first and foremost a wild and raunchy show about teenagers behaving badly. Set in 2004, the series follows the St. Mark’s dance team — go, Lions! — that initiates their newest member, Grace (Sofia Wylie), at a Halloween party held at an abandoned nunnery nicknamed Devil’s House because, as the myth goes, all the nuns who lived there went crazy. They all take ecstasy and offer Grace as a “prank” sacrifice to the devil so the team can make it to Regionals. But something terrible happens to Grace, setting off an infection of visions and religious hysteria across the team and the town that blurs the line between self-inflicted delirium and unexplainable phenomena. Trying to manage a gaggle of teenage girls and the church’s growing zeal is priest and school principal Father Franklin — whom the girls call Daddy Franklin — played by Nnamdi Asomugha as a stoic nearing his breaking point.

At the center of the mess is Lions’ co-captain Anya (Kristina Bogic, who brings pathos to the cheer captain trope) who, out of necessity, befriends Lisbeth (an excellently freaky Geena Meszaros), a new student who weasels her way onto the team and whose shady past seems to come in handy amid the chaos. Alongside weathering the hysteria and keeping secrets, Anya struggles deeply with her sexuality, refusing to admit her feelings for her best friend and co-captain Elise (Sara Boustany, playing one of the last bastions of sanity throughout the season) is anything more than something that happens when she’s drunk.

The Body is full of sex (and sexual repression) and partying that’s just a sidestep away from Euphoria or Elite, another one of Netflix’s horny high school series. Its litany of influences (or, at least, easy references to explain The Body) are numerous. It’s Yellowjackets (which returns for a final season later this month) if they never crash-landed in the woods. It’s Bring It On if it was overtly queer (so, But I'm a Cheerleader) and R-rated. The Mean Girls, duh. It has shades of the religious fervor found in movies like Carrie, Saint Maud, and The Testament of Ann Lee. Hell, it even has a little sprinkle of Ken Russell’s The Devils’ DNA. (Confess!) Shephard — whose previous work also grapples with the plight of young, often prickly women — channels these touchpoints and shapes them with her own voice into a series that feels immediately relatable yet fresh.

The show’s cast of under-the-radar young actors absolutely works to its benefit — though you might recognize Jackson Kelly, who plays Lisbeth’s brother Leo, as the troubled kid from Season 1 of The Pitt. Without the baggage of being known as “that person from that TV show,” the girls on the dance team, in particular, feel like… well, a Catholic high school girl’s competitive dance team. For as large as the ensemble is, most don’t come off as one-note. Shirley Chen is especially good as Maddie, a Lion who struggles with an eating disorder and intense Catholic guilt. But for a series about a dance team, there’s not nearly enough choreographed dance scenes. When the Lions finally perform at Regionals, it’s hard not to feel robbed of seeing more clever, funny, and beautiful sequences.

The Body is full of the demarcations of 2004: Razrs and Sidekicks, a Kelly Clarkson ringtone and general early aughts soundtrack, bedazzled track suits and bebe shirts, the background of the Bush/Kerry presidential election, and so on. Perennially, the student body mostly has rich parents. The series scratches at teenage conservatism and family wealth — a boy loudly celebrates Bush winning; Anya has an indoor pool and glam squad — but doesn’t go much further. Much like the teenagers themselves, The Body accepts these as just the way things are , focusing on the intensity of personal feelings. But given that the show has eight one-hour episodes, it could have used a little extra something in the back half as the inner turmoil becomes slightly repetitive.

As the last few episodes begin turning more surreal, The Body goes out on a nebulous ending that is equally frustrating and fascinating. It feels like it’s doing the obligatory streaming show thing, where a non-conclusive ending is an entry to more seasons if the data shows enough viewer interest. But it would certainly be a more interesting creative choice to end the show here and let viewers stew in the ambiguity.

If there's one thing that's true about any version of World of Warcraft, it's that Blizzard loves hiding convoluted quest chains behind mundane objects, the first of which has been found in WoW Forever.

If you've started a Skyborne character in Forever, you've probably completed a quest that rewarded you with an 'Ancient Heirloom' ring with no stats, and wondered why it even exists. Well, it turns out that it kicks off a whole hidden quest chain if you know where to look.

This secret was discovered by the WoW Secret Finding and Collections Discord , and it involves getting that ring, finding a sword hilt that only shows up when you're using a specific torch, then finding a blade with a random location and then finding and cleansing a 'Befouled Water Globe.' The community has put together a guide on Wowhead of the known steps so far, but there's a catch – it doesn't seem like anyone has actually finished the little scavenger hunt yet.

As of this morning, folks in the WoW Secret Finding Discord are still actively trying to see what gets unlocked at the end of this convoluted chain, but for now, the community is calling it the "Dawn Waker Secret" and seems to believe it revolves around a couple of swords: Eluvi'ana and Eluvi'tor.

As part of the process, you'll end up with a sword that you need to cleanse, and to do that, you'll need to clear the Capital Gardens section of Dire Maul and talk to Prince Tortheldrin, whose dialog hints that "such knowledge is reserved by those honored in my royal court." And, in classic WoW fashion, this probably means a lengthy rep grind is needed.

According to admin Miko in the WoW Secret Finding Discord, "Our most recent discoveries hint us that the rewards for this chain will involve the swords of Eluvi'ana and Eluvi'tor. The most recent step points us to a rep grind with the Shendralar Faction, as Prince Tortheldrin in Dire Maul tells us that only those Honored with his court are worthy enough to obtain the knowledge about these blades."

Depending on how long it takes players to actually get Honored with the Shendralar faction, it might be a while before the final reward is actually revealed. But there are hundreds of players in this Discord channel working on the secret, so it's only a matter of time.

We're still in the early days of WoW Forever, after all, and it's been a massively successful launch . And as more players start to get to max level , more secrets are sure to pop up in the world. After all, while World of Warcraft takes a lot of queues from Classic WoW, the developers have added a ton of content, so who knows how many secrets have been buried in the corners of Azeroth?

articles.title: How About a GTA Set Outside the United States? 'Never Say Never,' Rockstar Boss Teases, but Don't Hold Your Breath
articles.summary: Rockstar isn't ruling out a GTA set outside the United States, but don't hold your breath: the studio says there are plenty more stories to tell in America.
articles.body:
Rockstar isn't ruling out a GTA set outside the United States, but don't hold your breath: the studio says there are plenty more stories to tell in America.

In an interview with The Guardian , Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson was asked whether or not the developer would ever make a GTA game set outside of America. His response was simple: "Never say never." However, Nelson continued his response by stating, "There’s still so much to do in America."

The GTA series has largely rotated between three locations for the last 25 years: Liberty City (New York), Vice City (Miami), and San Andreas (California). We got a brief glimpse at the Midwest of GTA in GTA 5, when the game's story opened in a snowy state called North Yankton. But that's about as much as we've gotten outside of the coastal cities that GTA rotates through. It's unclear what else Rockstar wants to do with GTA, specifically the American setting.

GTA has flirted with going overseas before, as Rockstar came close to making one set in Japan in the early to mid-2000s . The first GTA also had an expansion set in London, and GTA 5 seemingly had scrapped DLC that would've at least partially taken place in Paris . Ex-GTA writer and creative director Dan Houser also stated last year that he doesn't think GTA would work as well outside of America .

"I think for a full GTA game, we always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else," said Houser. "You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere.”

Maybe one day it will happen, but it does seem like Rockstar's interests with GTA are rooted in American culture.

GTA 6 will, of course, take us back to Vice City next week when it launches on November 19. It is expected to have one of the biggest launches in history, with it already being the most preordered game in the history of Xbox and PlayStation's digital stores . Players are able to preload the game right now , and they absolutely should, as the game is a whopping 210 GBs.

articles.title: Nicholas Hoult's How to Rob a Bank Tries to Tackle Real-Life Problems But Fails to Make an Impact
articles.summary: How to Rob a Bank review: A movie with a lot on its mind that doesn’t do a very good job of articulating it.
articles.body:
How to Rob a Bank is in theaters beginning November 13.

Clearly, we live in notably crappy times in numerous ways, and clearly, there’s a lot to be fed up with about how the system seems so egregiously stacked against most of us while the rich constantly get richer. So sure, it’s good to have a big studio movie at least attempt to tackle these issues, but How to Rob a Bank never actually has enough to say about the topic except for reinforcing that yeah, this sucks, but hey, at least you can make some fun videos about it.

Nicholas Hoult stars as Ryan, the leader of a group of masked bank robbers who release elaborate videos of their crimes on the internet and have become online sensations as a result. Also filming rehearsed monologues to camera and tutorials on how to emulate their actions — titled, you guessed it, How to Rob a Bank — Ryan and his crew, which includes Emi (Anna Sawai), Vince (Pete Davidson), and Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz), make it clear in their videos that this is all about sticking it to ‘The Man’ and striking back against a world that’s made it so hard to get a financial foothold.

I have no doubt that people posting videos of themselves successfully carrying out a string of bank robberies would go viral, and yet How to Rob a Bank feels wonky from the start because of how overproduced and outright annoying these videos are. They’re filled with animation overlays, loud sound effects, and blaring music in what feels more like Hollywood filmmakers trying to evoke youthful, attention-getting videos rather than coming off as genuine. It doesn’t help that director David Leitch (Deadpool 2, The Fall Guy) sometimes also has this crew do impressive parkour-style flips in the midst of their heists and then gives zero explanation of how this would even be something in their skill set.

John C. Reilly plays FBI Agent West, the guy trying to bring in Ryan’s crew. He ends up recruiting the services of Reagan (Zoë Kravitz), who’s on home arrest after having been convicted of cybercrimes and whose knowledge, West believes, might be useful in tracking down the robbers. Reilly and Kravitz, and the very different energy they bring, actually make for a rather fun unlikely duo, and there are times where I found myself wishing we simply had a mismatched buddy cop-style adventure with them. But ultimately, both of their characters represent how How to Rob a Bank doesn’t follow through on many of the topics it’s bringing up.

Reagan is as anti-establishment as they come, clumsily represented by the stickers on her laptop that look like a checklist of progressive cause catchphrases, while FBI careerman West is very much part of the system. Reagan is also one of the ways the movie name-drops additional troubling and agonizing topics of the moment, from violent cops to school shootings, but even as the two inevitably start to begrudgingly get along, we don’t see either of them actually learn or change all that much in the movie. You might think there could be some drama in Reagan feeling empathy for Ryan’s crew — maybe even trying to help them from the inside — or that they could explore how West feels about being part of a system that can be used for corrupt purposes. But Leitch and writer Mark Bianculli never dig in enough to get more than surface level acknowledgement of anything of the sort.

This goes for the How to Rob a Bank crew as well, who are presented initially as a jovial, fun-loving team and each given a requisite single scene of their home life to try to ground them, with mixed results. Well, that’s except for two other guys in the group beyond the core four, who are so underutilized and often forgotten, it’s bizarre they’re included at all.

Inevitably, the movie takes the turn any story about a group of criminals must take, as the walls begin closing in on our modern day Robin Hoods (who do in fact give much of their stolen money to charity). There are a couple of late reveals about what motivates some of the crew — and how it impacts their past and future — that do carry some emotional weight, but those reveals are held off for too long, and the movie feels paper-thin for too much of its running time. And though they lead into a notably darker portion for a bit, even that feels pushed to the side by the conclusion, as though either the filmmakers or the studio (and yeah, it feels a bit, ahem, rich to have a story about financial inequality coming from Jeff Bezos’ Amazon) were afraid to leave things on too complicated a note.

There are times when you can enjoy the antics of How to Rob a Bank, helped along by its charismatic cast, and there are a couple of moments that shine, including a sequence where we see how the crew deals with being questioned by the cops which features a fun appearance by Young Mazino (Beef, The Last of Us) as their lawyer. We also briefly get moments where actors like Hoult and Sawai remind us that they can be dramatic heavyweights, but too much of the film feels like it’s mistaking loud and frenetic for making an impact as it lightly touches on important topics without actually doing the work to make them resonate.

articles.title: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.summary: The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 helped me track my fridge temperature and finally set up my in-wall speakers.﻿
articles.body: Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. And it’s working. I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs, and a pair of RS-232 serial ports. [Image: [Image: It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment. All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development. I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal. But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad. A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2. I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help. Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface. [Image: We love a setup wizard. In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again. The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total. I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem. I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up. [Image: You can’t go wrong. Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV. The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts. That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point. The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged. I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all. But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

articles.title: A Bard's Beloved - The Witcher 3 Guide - IGN
articles.summary: A Bard's Beloved is one of the stranger Side Quests you'll come across while exploring in Skellige. Unsurprisingly, the Side Quest revolves around a
articles.body:
A Bard's Beloved is one of the stranger Side Quests you'll come across while exploring in Skellige. Unsurprisingly, the Side Quest revolves around a Bard, but the "beloved" in question is someone that might end up making you somewhat surprised.

To help you complete this odd Side Quest, here's IGN's complete guide to A Bard's Beloved, including how to find the Side Quest and start it.

To start this Side Quest, you'll need to find a troubador in a cave in the east of Ard Skellig.

When you approach the troubador, he'll demand that Geralt is quiet as he heads into the cave, as his "beloved" is sleeping somewhere further inside and he really doesn't want to wake her up. Odd, but sure.

Head further into the cave and follow the path along; it's relatively linear.

Inside, you'll run into the Bard's bestie. Turns out, she's a level 15 Water Hag, and she'll greet Geralt by asking him for a rhyme.

No matter what you say to her, she'll leap and attack, so get prepared for a fight. This is where the Necrophage Oil comes into play. If you didn't apply it before the fight, do it immediately here.

Using Igni and Bombs will help you make light work of this enemy. Keep to her sides and back to avoid her main attacks, and watch for her key attack patterns. Greediness is the easiest way to die in fights like this, so only strike once her attack animation has finished.

Loot the body when she dies, then head back to the entrance of the cave. The troubador will be gone and the Side Quest will wrap up.

Your reward for finishing this Side Quest will be 25 x experience.

articles.title: A Death Metal Guitarist Is So Into WoW Forever, He Took it Onstage With a Steam Deck
articles.summary: World of Warcraft Forever is off to a monumental start, with more players wandering Azeroth than ever before. And at least one death metal guitarist can't put it down long enough to watch his opener play.
articles.body:
World of Warcraft Forever is off to a monumental start, with more players wandering Azeroth than ever before. And at least one death metal guitarist can't put it down long enough to watch his opener play.

Death metal band Archspire posted a video to Instagram, overlaid with text that reads, "POV World of Warcraft Forever comes out the same day as the show," as the camera shows a Steam Deck with an undead Warlock running around with his voidwalker. The caption carries on the bit, saying, "When your set starts at 9:00 but you just zoned into Undercity to pick up your Voidwalker quest so you can pet-tank your way through Fenris Isle."

I get the appeal, some of the quests in Fenris Isle are absolutely brutal if you don't have anyone else in your party, so getting a purple blob that can tank it for you really is exciting. It doesn't hurt that WoW Forever runs incredibly on a handheld, either.

WoW Forever's newfound controller support and lightweight system requirements make it a natural match for handheld gaming PCs. I've tested the game on both the Xbox Ally X and the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ , and both have been able to handle the game at pretty high settings without dipping below 60 fps. I haven't played the game on the Steam Deck quite yet, but at least from Archspire's Instagram post, it seems to be running just fine.

Archspire's guitarist is also not the only Death Metaller who loves WoW. IGN interviewed Cannibal Corpse way back in 2008 , and when we asked George "Corpsegrinder" Fisher about his love for the game, he told us, "It is true, I am obsessed with WOW! I have 70 level 70 characters. I play HORDE side ONLY. I hate the Alliance with a passion!"

Corpsegrinder also told us a story about how he was inundated with messages from fans, saying, "I did another interview where I said my Rogue's name and the server I played on, and then I started getting tells in game. A LOT OF TELLS. I was getting bombarded even when I was raiding, so I transferred him off the server and changed his name. I loved talking to people who were into Cannibal Corpse, but it was getting so I logged in and couldn't play, because all I did was exchange tells with people."

A lot has changed since 2008, but WoW Forever is looking to recapture some of that old-school WoW magic. And just based on how many people are playing the game, Blizzard seems to have pulled it off, even though they've run into some hurdles with gold rewards and dungeon experience .

articles.title: Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra Is Reportedly 'Close to Done,' Though at the Cost of Cutting Back on Content and Length
articles.summary: Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, Amy Hennig's Captain America/Black Panther game, is reportedly close to being finished, but it sounds like it may be extremely compromised.
articles.body:
Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, Amy Hennig's Captain America/Black Panther game, is reportedly close to being finished, but it could be extremely compromised.

According to a new report from Kotaku , Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is "close to done." The news comes hours after rumors began spread online that the game was canceled, with an official announcement coming soon. According to Kotaku and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, Skydancer leadership told staff via Slack that this is not the case and that they should continue business as usual.

Kotaku's report went on to describe the game's development as difficult, which should come as no surprise to anyone who's been following its journey. The title was announced in 2024 and has been delayed several times, with little to no news or footage beyond that.

Kotaku claims that Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra initially began as a Netflix game, but was later expanded for consoles and PC. Unfortunately, the title is reportedly "light on gameplay," with most of the action mapped to one button and the experience lacking "significant interactivity."

The project has also allegedly gone well over budget, and as a result, has had to "significantly" scale back from its original vision in terms of content and length. As of right now, we have no idea when Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra will release, but if it really is nearing the finish line, we could see something next year. Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like the game will be a hyper-engaging action/adventure title with riveting action, from the sound of it.

This is purely speculative, but based on the details from Kotaku's report, it wouldn't be surprising if this is more along the lines of a Quantic Dream experience like Heavy Rain or Detroit: Become Human, with some combat sprinkled in. Either way, if fans were hoping for something like Marvel's Spider-Man, but with Captain America and Black Panther, they may end up pretty disappointed.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is meant to be director Amy Hennig's first proper game since Uncharted 3 in 2011. Although she has consulted and helped out on some other games like Forspoken over the years, Hennig hasn't led a new game since Uncharted 3. She was reportedly ousted from Naughty Dog in the early 2010s after Uncharted 4 was struggling to meet internal expectations. She then went to EA, where she was meant to lead a new Star Wars game with Visceral Games, but the studio was shut down and the project was scrapped. Now, she's heading up this Marvel game... and we'll just have to wait and see how it turns out.
